projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with William H. Kelly was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II history of William H. Kelly. Mr. Kelly served in the US Army Air Force. He served state side, and his highest rank was corporal. I am Tom Swope, and this interview was recorded at Mr. Kelly's home in Medina, Ohio, on April 28, 2004. Bill was 86 at the time of this recording.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where were you living in 1941?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Let's see, next door was our -- was my parents' -- where I -- When we came to Medina -- We moved to Medina in 19 -- about, let's see -- 39. We had a large fox farm over in -- Maybe I shouldn't go into this.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, that is fine.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: In Geauga County, Thompson, Ohio, if you know where Thompson, Ohio, is.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: And my parents had raised silver foxes. And they developed a platinum fox. And also we had a mink farm. They were in fox farming. Dad started that when I was four years old in 1922. And so we moved over here in -- I think, we started in about '30 -- 1939. And I met this young lady in --

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: '41. Right, right.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: '41, right. Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So in 1941 you would have been -- let me do the math here. Maybe 23 years old?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Oh, I was born in 19 -- 1918.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes, so you would have been 22, 23, depending upon your birthday?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I assume you were out of school at that point, right?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have specific memories of December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Oh, very, very vivid. We were -- we were together, right? Right. When it hit, we were -- where were we?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: At my home.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Home, yes. We remember it very vividly, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Heard the news on the radio?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your reaction when you heard that news?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Well, I knew it was coming. I mean, and only -- the way it happened, it was devastating at Pearl Harbor. And it was -- challenge time. Right. FDR -- FDR's voice on the radio, you know, was -- was real -- that speech was almost amazing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you had been paying attention to the news and you could see that we were going to get into it?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right. Well, I knew they had been scrapping over in Europe, and it was just -- just waiting. And real -- No, no, I had several of my buddies from Hamrick College where I went that did sign up. I -- in fact, we -- we had such a chore with moving the ranch and everything that -- My parents were older, and it was -- it was my duty to carry forward, I guess. My sister was in the service. She -- she was in Red Cross in charge of the large Air Force Rest Home in __+ where the flyers come in to recoup after -- after their time and on the raids. And my brother was also in the service. He was overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: And so I was biding my time. And all three of us were in the service. Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And then you eventually were drafted?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When was that?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: In October -- let's see. October of '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: October of '44?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember doing anything in the years in between for the war efforts -- getting involved?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes. I was -- what you showed me the other day, the Air Raid Warden. And I had my -- I had my territory I covered, this quadrant of our community. And I should be cautious as I am saying this -- I don't know -- but we did have two, two families we were watching because they were of German heritage.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: And it was -- kept some track of.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Just kind of kept track of them and check in on them every once in a while?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right. Right. In the community.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have drills, air raid drills?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Oh, yes, yes. And I had to go -- when they sound their -- the alarm, why I had to go out and make sure everybody had their shades down. Some of them didn't cooperate the best, but I had a couple of fellows that just wouldn't do it. But most everybody did. Right. I remember before my sister went overseas, too, when she left to go from home into New York, I took her downtown to leave. And they had a blackout in Cleveland and you absolutely -- they put something in the chimneys of the factories, evidently, but you absolutely couldn't -- you couldn't see a sign, a sign post. I got lost coming out of Cleveland. I finally had to ask the guy. I got down on the drive, because I usually came through that way. And I -- I really had to have him -- in fact, he went with me to get me back out, down the path for home coming out. But it was -- I never saw -- it was an artificial, where they just, evidently -- I doubt that you could even see the city from the sky right at that time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did they do anything to any of the people locally that didn't pull their curtains down or whatever? Did they report them or fine them?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: We reported them. But, no, they didn't. No. They just were -- you always had somebody that, you know -- Everybody cooperated well other than, I think, there was two families, two -- two men really that just didn't think it was something that -- Didn't worry about it, they said. They didn't worry about it. Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Obviously they didn't bomb Medina. But were there any wild rumors about anything like that, that you remember?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: No, other than prepared -- being prepared. I had a certificate you found not too long ago of my air raid, my --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Your air raid warden certificate?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: My air raid warden certificate, right. Didn't you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get involved in scrap drives or anything like that?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Drives?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes. We were in the bond fund drives. And in fact over by a hospital -- I haven't been in the hospital for 35 years, board. And we brought the bond house out and put it on some property, on the right side of the hospital. It has the bond -- where they sold bonds. It was in the park at Medina. And the house is still over there, and it has the bond house that is on the front of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is that the actual bond house there? I have seen it.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: That was up in the park.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I have never stopped to actually go look at it, but I have seen it when I drive by.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right, right. But there were -- and that was our -- I believe -- I mean, their first raising bonds and -- and it took turns servicing the operation, you know, building there. Right. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you say you were drafted in October of '44. Is that right?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: That is right. Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I forgot to write it down. What branch of the service?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: I ended up in the Air Force.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right, right. I went into North Bend in -- this is North Bend. But you can see it -- My induction -- I went over to North Bend in Harrison. And having the animals, I had a good background in nutrition. And they had a dog kennel over there of about 40 dogs that they were training for in the field for -- for in the service. And I went down there one day, and they -- I said like -- I thought -- I thought with my background I thought, boy, it would be nice if I could get into the canine corp and work with the dogs, especially on nutrition. And I -- I got a show of duties, you know, where you hit the base. But I was able to go down. Then the next day they said they were -- what time the colonel would be there and I should come at 2:00 in the afternoon or something and he would be there. They would not let me see the kennel. The entry to the kennel and the kennel was a mess. The dogs were -- what they were feeding them, they were just -- it was just a mess. And I told him that I -- I would be interested in the canine corp and which he was involved in. And so they kept me an extra month from shipping me out of there. And I -- he asked: Can you help us out. I went out in the kennel and the dogs were just -- the stools were just -- it was just a mess. And I said, gee, there is just no need for that. You know, if you feed them right then they will have good stools. And then I -- I called my dad. And of course we have -- we always got meat supplies from the stock yards, meat and liver and pork. And we made our ready mix food for our foxes. And so I said: Can you -- And we use __ cereal, ___ cereal, cereal base. And I called dad and I said: Can you send over a supply of products for me and so I could make the supply. I went down -- they got a great big bathtub for me, and I -- metal -- and he brought the products over. And I mixed them up. And then within, oh, five days they were straightened out. But the kernel was such a mess, I said, you are going to have to clean this up, because -- and that is one reason they kept me. One other thing was they had round worm and they were not worming them properly. And so I -- they had brought some of a medication over for the project. And short story, after a month, the lieutenant colonel told me that I would be shipping out and going to Utah for basic. And said "secret orders," you couldn't -- it was all secret orders. And he said check me before you go though. I didn't check with that colonel, I thought it was -- I took for granted that is where I was going and going out there. They -- I guess I made the statement, I said, well, I am going. I didn't tell him where. Well, anyway we got -- we went West. And I know two of us were off the train in Kansas City when President Roosevelt passed away. And we were -- they let us get off to -- and I was one of them to get the papers to bring back on our troops saying going to.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was the reaction of the other people when they heard that news?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Oh, well, it was -- it was a strike. It was -- it was difficult to lose him and it was -- we didn't know just what -- how -- how much as I appreciated President Truman. I guess he had then the war, but it was going -- But they -- anyway, going out, I was -- I was dropped off on the Buckley Field, Colorado. They scratched me. And they called back for reclassification, and I had to talk to the lieutenant colonel. And the only way I could do it was to go back to the ground forces and be reclassified. And I said no, I was going to stay there. And it was good for me.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why did they -- why did they change you when you got to Denver, Colorado?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Well, they do that. They were doing that a lot of the times to fill --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- other jobs?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: -- jobs. Right. And I -- it was -- and I just -- I thought I was -- had to go West. I headed for basic in Utah. And it was a change of orders, right. And I looked at the orders, and they just put an X, you know, and changed my orders and shipped. And so I had my basic in Buckley Field. And then I -- I was -- went up to Strike Field in Wisconsin, and took radio school, and where we were working on -- and I was not very mechanical as such. It was quite a challenge to me, to work with -- So I was a nutritionist, not a -- a -- in working in that field. But it was, it was really good for me. And I -- we made the -- they were working on, up there -- The reason I was in -- it was ship-to-shore or we were using plane-to-plane operation where they could -- you could bounce the signal in flight. And that was my, my training and track. And then I went to Chanute Field from there in Illinois, and that was in electronics. And it was, well, the equivalent, they said, of a -- I had a 15,000 dollar education at that time in electronics. And I worked hard, I was in the libraries, because it was -- I -- I was not adapted to that type of being in the lab. Really. And from there I went to __+. We were married in December of '34 --

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: That is 50 years ago this year.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: And she was a war bride and followed me, followed me to the bases and both the tracks. And then after we were married and then to -- we were engaged, of course. And she -- to Chanute and Boca Raton. And I was placed in special group. I didn't realize at the time going in there that it was a special group. My first detail after, when I adjusted in, I think after the first two weeks there, where they had a big search set up in the dome of the Boca Raton Country Club, and it was searching the water off the coast because you couldn't walk on the beach, it was so oiled. But the Germans -- this was never known in our country -- the German subs were awaiting our boats or tankers as they came in from the Caribbean off the Coast. And we had -- we played tag with a submarine out there for about 25 miles off -- about where the Gulf Stream goes through, there is a ledge, and they lay under there, they were setting where we had ?PT boats?, I think it was planes going out, flying out. Our air base wasn't on the camp -- on our -- we were in Boca, we were completely __ listening out from the skies. We were -- we down in the Everglades down ___+ because we had six research men from the top electronic companies at that time there, and they -- they each had their own -- they built them -- their own labs separate on the base for -- where they were working on the television. And I was in the -- saw the first television wave at that time because I happened to be in the -- and we were in that night to the library. And I always would go over with them, because they were teaching us. And but, anyway, I was -- and I went over and calibrated this set every morning and -- make sure it was operating. Two of us would always go over and -- to the set. We had a hurricane later and they put everybody in that club. I don't know if -- we never got caught the second night -- it was bedlam. But the hurricane came in, and it hit us both ways. It came in, and then it came back out. And it was about 30,000 of us in that. They were just man to man -- and ladies. Some of the nursing crew and so forth were there. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: During the war you were flying patrols? Right?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were flying patrols sometimes, sub patrols, is that what you said?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Well, they had -- they had sail -- the Navy, they had about every thousand yards stationed all along the beach --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: -- at that time. And you couldn't walk on the beach. It was just like tar.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why was there tar on the beach? From the ships?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Because they would knock the boats out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: How many did they sink around there, do you have any idea how many tankers?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: I -- I really don't know. I -- we did catch the boat -- they did catch the boat. I was not involved in that. But they did catch a sub up on the top. I kept saying all the time, these guys on -- we had a lot of those men come in, when he was having the chase with Patton. And all of the prisoners came in down to our base. And we were not supposed to talk to them, but they could talk better English than I could. But they were there -- just the top, top people. But we did. They caught them on top and they put up a white flag and we took them. And that was never reported by -- at that time, because they didn't want to scare people. And they were cautious. In fact our operation -- we didn't even dare talk about it, we were ___+ in the club there -- with the people that were in the club area. And so from there I went on into the -- there was 13 of us that were in that was selected. And we worked on the radar bomb site using the atomic bomb. And my dad called me one day and says: What has happened to you? He says: The CIA has been here, the secrete service. He says: What is up? And kept calling. And I said: Dad, I cannot say anything. And I was followed for months off -- every time off the base. The only thing was -- researching was the site and the out of bounds -- was not to go to Miami, because everybody at the base was heading for Miami over the weekends. And I went, went up and went to Miami. And they -- But every time I was followed. Ruth never, never knew that. But every -- they would pick me up if we went out someplace. Yes, I knew they were --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You could see them?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes, I knew they were -- well, we knew they were. We knew we were being followed. But --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Why did they want you to avoid Miami in particular, just because of the city?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Oh, it was bedlam, and what was going on down there. Just getting down there and getting jumped or something. It was always that we couldn't, couldn't -- couldn't drink. I mean, we were under, under secret orders.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So there was no partying for the group, your guys in your group?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: No, no, no. It was -- like I say, the wives didn't even know that we were being followed.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you know what you were doing?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: I knew we were on an arm of the Manhattan group. But -- and I -- it was -- Here was my -- (sound of paper) see what we got.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is that your discharge?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: I thought I had it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Here it is. Here. Yes, this, this was my -- this was my -- I had been -- I had completed my project for a month.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: And this was my service record. And this was my -- my -- I was -- the __ bomber, the __+ 23 that we were on the atomic bomb radar side. We used an atomic bomb. I would have been fine -- I was scheduled to be flying within the month.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes. Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You said you were trained to operate this?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Operate this radar?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes. Right, right. I was always glad I didn't have to because I -- It bothered me because they dropped the bomb on population. You know, I felt possibly they could have done it on military, but -- and a couple of years it really bothered me, because I was involved with it so closely -- and of the operation. We were flying over from Boca to New Mexico. Of course that is where the headquarters of the operation was. And it was -- it was quite a crude operation. I imagine it was -- I don't know how -- a bag of flour, I don't know how -- maybe it was two tons, three tons, I cannot remember at that time. But, anyway, we would fly over and drop it on the target. And, of course, we were flying at 40,000 feet. And because when we dropped it, if we -- if we hit the target, it exploded. And we could see. What a crude thing -- but we could see how close we hit the target. And working on it. But I had -- I hadn't -- I knew it was something secret, but I, I -- and powerful. But we didn't know. Of course it wasn't released until they dropped the bomb. But we were --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now, you would have -- you say you were scheduled to fly if the war had continued, right?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes. Yes. And I thought surely we had another, you know, four, five years in going island to island in Japan. I really was, was prepared to -- I had no idea. That is why I say, I really appreciated President Truman's guts, because --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Now what kind of bombing do you think you would have been doing if you had kept flying, if the war had continued?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: It would have continued.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You would have dropped another atomic bomb?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes, it would -- yes, that was what I was training for, right, right, in the radar operation. And we had -- it was the first scope -- the oscillated scope for -- it was -- that we could -- we could take readings on. But I was -- it was -- we trained for the mechanics of the scope and for the operation of it. Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember any big celebrations on VJ Day?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Oh, boy. We had a bear -- we had a -- we brought us a 1932 Chevy for down there, and I drove it back and forth to the base. We lived in Del Ray Beach. I lived off the base. And, boy, we had everybody on top of the -- on the fenders, around the -- we used to have running boards. And that was -- And we went down to --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: West Palm Beach. THE WITNESS: Yes, West Palm Beach. And, boy, we snaked in. And, boy, it was hilarious. Just --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: Happy day.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes. Because the pressure was just so extensive at that time. And I know in, in the -- in the base at Boca, they were giving tests. And I had to take the test every Monday morning, because -- when the bell tolls. And they were one of the -- for the Kaiser ships that were carrying supplies. Of course they were -- didn't have much of a rudder on them. And -- but they would give tests. And if you swamped out, why they shipped you out. And I know a couple of them were, got word back to us: But don't get on one of these things. I guess they rode like a bathtub, I guess, in the water. But -- but they operated the electronics part of the -- on the Kaiser ships is what they were -- they were taught, assigned to do. But everybody was sweating blood. Every Monday morning, after they went around for almost, almost five weeks. They would give a test. And none of us, none of us would keep the -- we would all had to take the test ___+. But that was -- And, in fact, we had the car when they were -- they were bringing so much of the wounded through Boca at the hospital there. Then they were -- anybody should have a -- any way out to -- lucky like we had an automobile. We made it back to Paris to be discharged, right of going. But it was --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So when were you discharged?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: In October of '45.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you only had to serve a year; is that right?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: A year, sixteen months.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right, right, right. Oh, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you have any -- obviously you had a wife, but did you have any close buddies when you were in the service?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Oh, yes, we had great guys. Yes, right. Right. There was a lot of camaraderie. And of course especially with the fact that the fellows did allow us to have our wives to travel and, you know, to live off base. And had to get a job.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: If they could find a job.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: If they could find a job. And she -- it was -- it was quite a celebration though. But, anyway, we were able -- and I don't know -- We had a flat tire coming home, and I -- and in Jackson -- I got to Jacksonville on the spare, and the guy from -- wouldn't -- I was supposed to be able to get repairs, and this guy wouldn't -- he held off. And finally the two gals in the office said: You come back after 4:00 when he leaves and we will take care of you. So I got my oil and my spare tire repaired and we got back to ?Patterson -- but, it was a great -- it was an experience that was -- I always wished I had been in the canine corp where I could do that part. But it really did me good because I learned a new business that we have -- why -- I came home. We -- we discontinued the ranch. My parents -- we were -- I don't know how old they had been. Their health was going. My mom's health. And we discontinued the ranch. So I had some in electronics. I really didn't want to live a lifetime in the four walls of the lab. I mean, I was an outdoor boy. And so we -- this was down to about 38 dollars of severance pay. And we had the grinders and the mixers and the freezers and the coolers and everything from our fox farm, and we started Bil-Jac Foods and in the pet food business. And it was -- it has been quite, quite an adventure. I am being inducted this Saturday night in the Medina --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: -- Chamber of Commerce Hall of Fame.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: -- Chamber of Commerce Hall of Fame for my adventure. But certainly the war service was quite an adventure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I was going to ask you. So you started Bil-Jac Foods?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes, I am the Bill.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You are the Bill in Bil-Jac?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes. My brother -- my brother was Jack.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Your brother was Jack?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: And dad, my dad was a New York boy. And he knew a haberdashery in New York that was Bill Jack, and only he shortened it to Bil-Jac. I am lucky I have all three of my boys in the business, and we are now national and international in our company.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Very successful. But we started out with nothing. Start it all over again. I tell you, Ruth and I were down to our last of our severance pay. It was a gamble, because I didn't know. It was more of a premium dog food. I had to pay about -- charge about three times more than what was the middle was charging for ground up grain. And so it was -- But it was sort of a tragedy on my folks because -- to lose the business. It was tough.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: My dad's lifetime was shut down. I think he always suffered from it. Didn't he? Because they were -- after the war, dad never was absolutely -- closed the ranch down.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: He took it so hard.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: President Roosevelt died.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes, he really took that hard. And being a New York boy, he knew -- very close. Well, you had an association with your -- where you worked in Del Ray Beach and Roosevelt's --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: But that wasn't during the war.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Well, it was during the war. Wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: No. Well, I don't know just what you are referring to.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: The lady. You worked for the _ service there.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: She was a nurse.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: And she was a nurse.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: A nurse.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: Worked for President Roosevelt.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Really?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: And it was in __ Springs.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: She wrote letters back to the office all the time about President Roosevelt. She thought he was so wonderful.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You never got a chance to meet FDR?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you get back to the war, do any other particularly vivid memories come to mind?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: I guess -- knowing the secrecy of what I was in, and not knowing what it was, it was -- it was nip and tuck really, because we were under tremendous pressure really to get our training. And we had no idea that, you know, dropping two bombs would end the war. We really -- we really thought that in the course, within the month why she would have gone home and I would have been on my way. And I guess that was the biggest pressure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you speculate at all what you think -- what you were doing, the top secret job was? Did you have any guesses?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: No. Not -- not that big. We knew -- we thought we were a block buster type bomb or something, but we had no idea --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What you had?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: -- involved in that. And we knew there would be an action and we were being trained for that. And it was pressure time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Pressure time.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And I have read that eventually Tokyo would have been one of the targets --

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- if it had continued?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes. They would have been hit, right. Right. But I was -- my orders are, I would have been assigned -- I say, I was a month out. And we would -- I was the number three man of the twelve that was left going out. And so they told me that I was -- we would have been assigned for -- within the month at that time. So I was -- when I saw -- I really -- It had to be tragic what happened over there. But it was -- but it stopped it. It was amazing. Just really -- everything was being prepared, you know, to continue it, with the scrap, and it was -- they were going down our smoke stacks. And one of boys went out and was killed. And it was -- My best friend was killed. He was on the run with Jimmy Dougle, on the run into Tokyo. And he was -- they had a head courier of Cleveland. And he was -- ran out of fuel and went down, and they captured him and he died of malnutrition. And it was -- just one of those instances where -- tough.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right. Bobby Major is a nice prince of a guy.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Was he from Cleveland or Medina?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: He was from Cleveland?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes. He had a ___+ from Cleveland, it was a shame. Of course being in the food business, I was close to him and knew him real well. And one of my best friends from college ?Carl Krafts? Was killed in Europe which is -- it is all a hollow feeling, right -- And I think there was pressure with us. I mean, we had a lot of pressure.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: I am sure glad he wasn't on that plane that dropped the bomb though.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: He could have been --

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: But it was amazing. I asked her not too long ago again if she had ever realized that we were being followed off base.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: I cannot --

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: And how --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: I was just so happy to be with him.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: But we couldn't -- you know, it was all secret orders. And, boy, it was strict. I mean, we couldn't speak a word of it even, even out in the -- on the base because all -- we were completely separate from --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: When they called your dad to ask what was going on, what were they doing with him, checking with him about?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: My dad -- __+ of my background.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: What kind of a guy I was, I guess, before I was classified into this. I was being classified into the project.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: But -- so, I had a best friend -- fellow he asked -- interviewed me last year, going to Akron U -- What is the last name? Brandon -- And he, he wrote his information off about the people on the home front, the military and the home front, the job that they did to, you know, make it successful. And it wasn't just an overseas operation. But I -- I know I didn't want to go on the ground forces. But that is the end of my story. And, by the way ?owner of Buckley Field?, our staff sergeant was the head of our unit, we got him another bar -- because we marched so good. And then our basic was a -- going out to bivawack, the 25-mile hike, it was 120 that day. But it was less than a third of us finished the trip. They had ambulances out there picking up the guys. If I hadn't had two Heath Bars and three bottles of Coke, I don't think I would have made it. Set up camp. And had a tragedy out there, too. B-51s were scraping us all the time. When they were going out, we would have to leave the road and go in the -- fall flat on the ground. And we were out there and in south camp, and one of them came over and he lost altitude and went down and crashed. And I volunteered, I guess because I was used to handling horse meat and meat and so forth. I volunteered to help pick him up. We picked him up in a duffle Basket. It was just terrible. So that was a -- well, a big tragedy at that time. It was something those guys would come over and, man, they would swoop through. And there was good old training.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other stories like that that you remember from your training?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Is what?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Any other stories like that that you remember? Not certainly like that. But any other stories that you remember from your training?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: I guess basically it was the privilege of working with these research people that was -- that were teaching us the mechanics of -- they were just outstanding research people. And I knew every one of them. So -- I lived with them practically. And it was just, just a -- a great experience. And -- I -- I often think the way the electronics was going, the use of the scope and everything, my background, I wonder where I would have gone in electronics. With the pet food -- but --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: But I -- and I truly didn't like the ?40F?, I just -- working in the lab, it was just -- And the oscillator we were working on was a rascal because it was -- to calibrate it it would go off cycle. And it was what we call just a -- a couple of them called them bastards. But, I mean, because they were just so temperamental. But it was a scope that we could read distance and get all -- and of -- of course, the bombardier of the plane took over the plane on the run. I mean, it -- the time when it hit throughout the instrument, why you were in charge of the operation which -- which we were trained for. Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were trained as a bombardier, too?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Well, I was a bombardier.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, I thought you said you were a radar?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Well, but the operator, I was the operator of a radar set that was going, pulling --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were --

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: We were pulling the trigger.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It was more high tech at that point?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: We were pulling the trigger, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I will read this here from your separation qualification record. "Maintain and operated high altitude of radar set, made minor repairs and adjustments, was in the operation of DynaMotive Amplidynes." Is that right?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: "Motor generators and deloys"?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right, right, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I guess I don't know this stuff. "Was familiar with basic electrical circuits, vacuum tubes, theory of operation."

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Of course, that was a vacuum tube type.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So the B29's were dropping bombs, bombs by radar?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes. Right, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Is that the one, that you go to two atomic bombs that were dropped on?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right, right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And in theory it would be more accurate?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes. Well, yes, they -- they were. Right. It was up and coming unit that -- that they -- and a new unit that they were head -- were -- had worked on for the -- for the use. Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I don't think they used those on other bombers, do they?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: No. No. Although the bombardier, as I say, usually was in -- when -- at the time, going into the period of a short time of when he dropped the bomb, it was -- because he had -- he had to say I am going to pull --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: -- you know, pull the trigger.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes. Yes, exactly.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: But I was always glad that it stopped -- the war stopped, I didn't have to go into it, have to do it. I just -- what happened for the populace over there was tremendous. Right. So -- But there was a lot of pressure. And I -- I just -- constant pressure because you never knew when you were going to be shipped.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: I mean, they could -- they could scratch you and out you go. I mean, over -- I would say two-thirds of the -- of the unit that were at Boca with me or were -- had gone. And there was not very many of us left. Me and -- my neighbor were assigned out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: And mostly the Kaiser ships, because they were -- those other ships. I mean, there was -- electronics was ship-to-shore and so forth, ship-to-ship. Right.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: There was one thing, when you ask about what our reaction was when we heard about --

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: The end of war?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: FDR?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: No --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The bombing of --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- the atomic bombs?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: Yes -- no.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Or Hiroshima or -- What? What did I ask you?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: No. My mind is going, too.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I think I asked you about your reaction to FDR, to VJ Day.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: No.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you found out what an atomic bomb was maybe?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: No. When they bombed over at --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, Pearl Harbor, sure.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: When we were together. Did I understand you to say you sort of knew it was going to happen?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: No. Well, I knew that we were preparing for war.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: Yes, but that was a complete surprise.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes, yes, it was. Coming from --

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: Pearl Harbor.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: -- coming from Japan especially.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: Well, I got it -- because he said that he --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, I heard that before. You just -- You could sense that we were going to get into a war, headed for war?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: We were for two years over there. You know, England and --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: It was.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: And we kept hearing more each day because, you know, we didn't have television and everything. And right at the first report, bombing of Pearl Harbor. But we heard more each day. It just kept getting worse, as we heard it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: As you heard more on the news?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Mrs. Kelly
sp.p: I just wanted to set that straight.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, because we were cutting off trade with Japan and we were just kind of pushing them. Well, they deserved it.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Well, their representative was in Washington when it happened. I mean, they were -- it was.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They were supposedly negotiating?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right. Negotiating. And they had -- I had one fellow, that was interesting, Bob Hubble, in Hyram When I was there was -- they set up a -- oh, I don't know what I want to say -- a government in Japan to show them how we operated. He was secretary of state. And it was -- it was very interesting working with him, working over there and reports back of -- they were showing him our, our government process. And I guess the wonderful thing after the war was the Marshall Plan. They were so -- and it wasn't -- you know, I don't think you can buy anything. I think you have -- it is personal. And just like Bob being, setting up the government and the people went out in our nation as a whole healing from the wounds of that war. You know, we lost 460-some-thousand men. And of course we see the thing we are in right now which is not good. But, you know, one, one or two -- you know, this is on the paper and I just don't know how -- I expect the losses to be so much heavier over there because they are just -- this is terrorist stuff and -- I wanted to live through this century, because of what was developing. I could see in nutrition and, well, the computer -- what was coming. And I thought it would be just a greatest era of the world, really. And this terrorist thing is just a tremendous situation.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: I -- it is just going to be a long time to -- I was in business -- We had a, a nutrition business, and my background. And we had a plant and partnership with Beatrice Foods in Norway for -- Oh, how many years was I over there? Twelve years, I guess, back and forth. But I would go up -- We had soldiers in the hook of Norway, way up. And when I would be calling on the -- we were making protein for their mink and fox. And also the farmers were raising salmon in the fjords, down, way down, to even freeze. It is cold over there. And when I was up, way up north __+ in fact the first time I went up there, they always said you could read a newspaper at 2:00 in the morning. I set my alarm and went outside, outside where I --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: -- read the newspaper?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: -- where I could read the newspaper. But I would always go up and see the guys up there, because they would be -- 25,000 of them. They would go from there and then they would go into Germany in rotation. And it was no man's land up there. But we -- the Russians were -- Well, it was something. They have mafia that was just terrible. And they were more afraid up there of the mafia than they were of the Army -- of infiltration. And it was just the pressure they had up there because --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Where was this?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: This was in the cold war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: During in the '50s?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Huh?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: During the '50s maybe?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: No, it would have been in the '70s.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: During the '70s. Oh, wow.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right. And it was -- it was -- but they were more afraid of the mafia than -- of infiltrating -- than they were, because they were just so -- they were just so organized. And there was a -- But they always took some messages back from them and they always liked to see Americans up there. It was interesting.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right. Really. And then dealing with a socialistic country, it was -- my father, we -- it had -- My parents had bought their first silver fox from ?prince at arms?, Charles Dalton, to develop the silver fox from -- it is not a wild animal, while it was developed genetically from a red fox. And he said there would be a different fox dog face developed. And he gave them the pro forma. And this is the first round. And the second round 1933, it hit. We had two little platinum foxes to go along with our silver foxes. And they had developed the red platinum fox. It so happened because he since sent breeding stocks to ?Martin King? Family and sold them over there. And then when we got the plant half built they realized that you couldn't -- you couldn't buy a cup of coffee over there before 7:00 in the morning. And just a -- regulations. And everybody has to be out of the plane, you know. We lost a generation of people because if they made 18,000 dollars a year, they tax them 50 percent. And anything over that, 93 percent. And they truly lost a generation of people out of Norway because -- and they just begged to come to the United States with us. But we didn't, of course. But, anyway, he was -- the father was in the power line over there, and it took us almost nine months, and we finally got it through. And I would go with him into the plant, several times. And where he was getting it through so we could run two shifts, because where this shifts, which is a herring-type fish up in the -- if that they were catching on the North Sea was, they were -- only ran about 120 days a year. Well, we would go to mammoth silos to store them. But we could never catch enough fish in 120 days to run the plant. We were almost -- question of whether to shut it down. And it was quite an experience seeing how that socialistic countries were in control, were in -- I would always kid, I came home and kissed the ground. I kid. Right, because it was -- People are nice, they were wonderful people. But I felt so sorry for the older people because they were -- so many of the young, good young people were -- were, you know, had lost a country -- Germany, Europe. Terrible. Switzerland. And then of course they got their oil wells out in our sea. And it has helped their economics. But it was quite, quite a lifetime. Right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Well, very good.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Good.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: We went beyond the war a little bit.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: I hope I gave you a little information.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Oh, yes, very.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: I guess one thing you asked on pressure, I think the basic pressure we were -- we were under a lot of pressure. And it was a push to get our training in for what was coming. I mean, it was tremendous pressure at the base.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes. Because they wanted you ready for what was coming next, huh?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right. Well, what our job was -- we knew it was something special.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: And it was just -- and to get us through, get us trained was -- they were really -- it was, it was a lot of pressure.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And for quite some time as I understand, they just devastated Japan with fire bombing?

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Yes, that is right.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I mean, it was amazing that they didn't give up then.

sp.speaker: William H. Kelly
sp.p: Right. Yeah. Well, they just -- you know, they were -- they were not going to -- The service men I have talked with that were in this island-to-island planning stand-off were just -- oh, it was just terrible. I mean, it was just -- they were like animals almost. (End of CD.)
